sections.h2: Selling a house in Grand Forks
sections.html:
Grand Forks is the county seat of Grand Forks County, on the western bank of the Red River of the North where the Red Lake River joins it. It sits at 837 feet and covers about 29.3 square miles, 74 miles north of the Fargo-Moorhead area and 145 miles south of Winnipeg. The city grew from 1,705 residents in 1880 to 59,166 in the 2020 census, helped by early railroads and by the University of North Dakota, which opened in 1883. The Air Force base has brought thousands of jobs since 1954.

Higher education, defense and health care dominate the local economy, so owners who rented to students, faculty or service members are often selling after a tenant move rather than on a schedule they chose.

sections.h2: The 1997 flood and what it left behind
sections.html:
The April 1997 Red River flood devastated the city. It led to a new levee system and a greenway where homes once stood.

1997 flood measureFigure
Crest at East Grand Forks, April 2254.35 feet (flood stage 28 feet, 1979 record 48.8 feet)
Damage near Grand Forks and East Grand Forks$3.6 billion
Downtown buildings destroyed by fire, April 1911, including 60 apartments
Dike system cost, reported a decade later$400 million

The new levee system was finished about ten years after the flood and required relocating numerous residents. The old floodplain became the Greater Grand Forks Greenway. Ask your insurer and the city about flood zone status for any house near the river.

Basement moisture and sump pump function are sensible checks before listing. If your house took water in a recent spring, keep invoices and photos for the buyer.

Grand Forks has a warm-summer humid continental climate. Subfreezing temperatures have occurred in every month of the year, average precipitation is about 21.7 inches and snowfall about 48.4 inches. The record low is minus 43 degrees Fahrenheit and the record high is 109. Buyers pay attention to the roof, furnace and insulation for that reason.

Grand Forks requires a Certificate of Occupancy for rental units whether or not rent is collected, and one- and two-family rentals have faced a licensing requirement since 2006. The city inspects each rental about every five years, or sooner after complaints.

The inspection checklist is specific:

  • Heating that keeps each occupied room at 68 degrees, three feet above the floor
  • At least two off-street parking spaces, with more depending on bedroom count
  • Smoke detectors, egress, electrical wiring and handrails or guardrails to the code in effect when the building was built
  • No more than four unrelated individuals per unit
  • Junk or junk vehicles resolved before a certificate issues

Owners who do not comply can be cited in municipal court, and a judge may order a unit vacated. If you plan to sell a rental, check its certificate status first, since a buyer will ask.

sections.h2: The County Recorder's role in a sale
sections.html:
The Grand Forks County Recorder's Office records documents that affect title to real property, such as a deed, and keeps them permanently. It is at 151 South 4th Street, phone 701-780-8262.

North Dakota has no deed or mortgage tax. Copies cost $1.00 per page, and certified copies cost $5.00 for the first page and $2.00 for each additional page. Ask the office or your title company about recording fees.

Under North Dakota's disclosure law, a seller of a home with up to four units must disclose material facts in writing. Sales by a mortgagor in default, foreclosure sales and transfers by estate fiduciaries are exempt under Century Code 47-10-02.1.

Real estate tax across North Dakota can be paid in full by February 15 for a 5 percent discount, or in installments due March 1 and October 15. Call the Grand Forks County Treasurer to confirm the balance on your parcel. At closing, the title company pays the tax from your proceeds, so a payoff figure good through the closing date saves surprises.

sections.h2: Selling when you are behind on payments
sections.html:
A sale is possible at any stage before a foreclosure sale, and North Dakota's process gives you time to act. Foreclosure is judicial, the lender must usually give 30 to 90 days' notice before suing, and the borrower has 30 days from notice to reinstate.

After a sale, redemption generally lasts 60 days, and deficiency judgments are barred for owner-occupied residential property of four or fewer units on up to 40 contiguous acres. The federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act gives added protection to military personnel, which matters near the base. An attorney can walk you through your options.

If you want a quick sale, a cash offer buys the house as it stands, and we make no promise of a price before seeing it. Compare it with listing, factoring in repairs, commissions and time.

sections.h2: What to line up before closing
sections.html:
Three numbers decide what you take home from a Grand Forks sale: the mortgage payoff, the county tax balance and the Recorder's fees. Request each one early, and ask that it be good through your closing day. If the house is a rental, add the Certificate of Occupancy status to the list.

  • Mortgage payoff letter from your lender
  • Tax balance from the Grand Forks County Treasurer
  • Certificate of Occupancy and inspection history, for a rental
  • Flood insurance and flood zone information, if the house is near the river
  • Your deed, or the estate paperwork if you inherited

With these papers gathered, a buyer or title company can tell you quickly what you would net, whether you list or sell for cash.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works here
sections.html:
A cash buyer takes the house as it stands. You do not make repairs, stage rooms or hold open houses, and no lender appraisal stands between the offer and the closing. That helps when the house needs work, when a tenant has just left, or when a military move or job change sets your deadline.

The paperwork still runs through a title company. It checks title, collects the tax payoff and any mortgage payoff, and pays them from your proceeds. The Recorder's Office then files the deed. If the house has flood history, rental problems or deferred maintenance, a cash buyer prices those in from the start, so you do not negotiate repair requests after an inspection.

Compare any offer with the cost of listing: repairs, commissions and the months of carrying costs while you wait for a buyer's loan.

faqs.q: Is Grand Forks still at risk of flooding?
faqs.a: A new levee system was completed about ten years after 1997, and the old floodplain became the Greenway. Ask the city and your insurer about your parcel.

faqs.q: Does Grand Forks require rental licensing?
faqs.a: One- and two-family rentals have been subject to a licensing requirement since 2006, and every rental needs a Certificate of Occupancy.

faqs.q: Is there a deed tax when I sell a Grand Forks house?
faqs.a: No. North Dakota has no deed or mortgage tax. Recording and title fees are separate.

faqs.q: What happens if I miss mortgage payments in Grand Forks?
faqs.a: The lender usually sends a notice 30 to 90 days before filing suit, and you have 30 days to pay the past-due amount. A judge must approve a foreclosure sale.

faqs.q: When are Grand Forks County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Real estate tax can be paid in full by February 15 for a 5 percent discount, or in installments due March 1 and October 15. Call the Treasurer for your balance.
